newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-S.AFRICAN LABOUR IN POWER PLAY WITH GOVT.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-S.AFRICAN LABOUR IN POWER PLAY WITH GOVT.

text.p: South Africa's biggest trade union grouping threw down the gauntlet over labour legislation last month, threatening a national stayway, but analysts believe government will sidestep a serious clash with its labour allies.

The 1.5 million member Cosatu trade union federation said it planned a national stoppage in May over the Employment Standards Bill which deadlocked in tripartite negotiations with business and government.
But any mass-action is expected to be low-key with pragmatic union leaders unlikely to provoke an all-out confrontation.

"What we've seen from Cosatu is an attempt to bring the labour-related legislation to the front of the agenda while government is not in a hurry to pass the legislation and may well leave it sitting on the backburner," says industrial relations consultant Andrew Levy.
Cosatu is likely to make its point by threatening mass action but in a low-key way which is almost certain not to culminate in national strikes, he said.
"I think Cosatu is building negotiating capital at the moment...they're building a bargaining position."
Employment law is just one area of friction between unions and the ANC government whose market-oriented Growth Employment and Redistribution (GEAR) strategy has angered some trade unionists.

While financial markets complain about foot-dragging on the implementation of GEAR, Cosatu insists that large parts of the plan -- such as privatisation and the phased elimination of exchange controls -- are hostile to workers and the poor.
Some commentators have warned that "crunch-time" is looming but on the whole tension around GEAR is not seen manifesting itself in a damaging showdown.

Says Karl von Holdt, senior researcher at Naledi, the research policy institute sponsored by Cosatu: "There's going to be a mixture of talking and fighting...quite what the mixture will be is difficult to say.
Struggles are likely to centre around areas where GEAR has clear consequences for labour such as privatisation of state assets.
"What we can expect are struggles over the goals and implementation of policies rather than a high profile confrontation over GEAR," says von Holdt.
DELIVERY CRUCIAL FOR GOVERNMENT CREDIBILITY

Banking group Nedcor chief economist Dennis Dykes says 1997 is a key year for delivery: "We've spent the last couple of years on policy formulation and it now comes down to delivery on key areas such as exchange controls and housing."
Government's balancing of labour and business interests can be sustained if it manages to deliver on all fronts, Dykes says."It's crucial that they fall into place at the same time."

Cosatu's latest contribution to the economic debate came in November. Its economic policy discussion document -- "A Draft Programme for the Alliance" -- focused on state activities and private sector issues requiring state regulation. Among other things it proposed a policy to lower interest rates, wage-restraints on the higher-paid and a national health service.

The document was largely ignored by the financial markets on the grounds that the policies laid out contradicted sound economic management. But, says a commentator in the left, some of the policies do not necessarily contradict GEAR. They are "germs" of what will become coherent, powerful Cosatu policy positions, he argues.

Von Holdt says Cosatu is exploring policy options other than the government's growth plan. "GEAR rests on policies not proven to be the only way to deal with the challenges of the global economy," he says.

In addition, the union movement doubts that GEAR can deliver the kind of targets that it projects, quite apart from other key developmental type issues like building an effective national health system. GEAR aims to double economic growth to six percent and create an annual 400,000 new jobs by 2000.
But those on the left do not criticises everything in GEAR.

"A positive about GEAR is that it has investment components and talks in quite strong terms about state-led public investment as well as private sector investment...for Cosatu that will be an important aspect to build on," von Holdt says.
SOCIAL CRISIS VERSUS FINANCIAL MARKET CRISES
Financial commentators say the economic debate is driven by the overwhelming power of the global markets.

Says one senior economist at a leading bank: "Essentially South Africa has very little choice in what it does. We have to implement GEAR energetically and enthusiastically or the world will gradually lose interest."
But the argument is multi-faceted.

"The drama that business is seeing is not the only drama that's on the stage...there may be a direct contradiction between what the people of South Africa wantin terms of delivery and what the financial markets want," says von Holdt.

For the labour movement the challenge lies in fleshing out coherent and powerful policy positions and to develop a pro-active vision for the restructuring of state assets, says von Holdt, moving away from the "reactive mode" it has been in.
"It's essential for Cosatu to go in with a proactive vision and set of policies...that will be critical in shaping the way things turn out in the next few years," he says.
-- Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
